caption:

What I forgot is that athletes never train without recovery. Rest days are scheduled. The programme decides, not the mood on the day.

caption:

Build the map in an afternoon. List every decision that reached you in the last two weeks, and next to each, who should own it and the rule they'd follow. Discounts under a set amount. Scope changes under a set number of hours.

caption:

line: busy isn't a business model.
caption:
A full calendar feels like proof the business is working. Often it shows the business can't run without you.

Sort next week's calendar into three colours. Green: only I can do this, and it's high value. Amber: someone could do it with a rule or a recording. Red: this shouldn't exist.

Cancel one red. Hand over one amber. Protect every green. Repeat next week.

line: you don't need a bigger team. you need fewer decisions.
caption:
When founders feel stretched, the instinct is to hire. Often that adds a manager to your week, and the manager is you.

Count first. For one week, tally every decision you make for the business: pricing a custom request, approving a design, choosing a supplier, deciding which client goes first.

Then sort them. Which could a written rule decide? Which disappear with one standard offer? Which belong to a role that already exists? The hire you need after that is usually different from the one you planned.

line: the goal isn't more revenue. it's more of it reaching you.
caption:
Three numbers tell you more than revenue: what you pay yourself, what's left as profit, and how many hours it took.

A simple target for 2027. Pick a founder salary you'd be proud of. Pick a margin to keep, often 20 to 30% for a service business. Pick the hours a week you want to work. Then design backwards. Which offer delivers that margin? Which clients fit it? Which work comes off your plate?

line: Delegating more won't fix a business built around you.
caption:
You delegated. It came back. You delegated again, more carefully. It came back again.

Delegation breaks in three predictable places. No written standard, so the work comes back for checking. No decision rule, so the person asks before acting. No ownership, so they're doing tasks while you still hold the outcome.

Fix those first. Write what good looks like with one example. Write what they can decide without you. Hand over the whole outcome. Then let them get it slightly wrong a couple of times.

line: Booked out isn't success if you're the only one booked.
caption:
“Fully booked until March” sounds like the dream. If every booking needs you personally, it's a waiting list for your exhaustion.

Being fully booked is the best moment to redesign, because demand finally gives you options. Raise the price on a defined offer. Bring someone in to deliver part of it. Say no to work that doesn't fit.

Ask which parts of what you're booked for genuinely need you. Usually the strategy, the key conversation and the final review. The rest is process.

line: You built the business. Now build the one that runs without you.
caption:
The first version runs on the founder's energy. It has to, because you're sales, delivery and operations.

The second runs on structure. The shift usually starts between $30K and $80K a month, when the business is busy enough to feel successful and heavy enough to feel unsustainable.

The order I'd rebuild in: the offer, then who owns which decisions, then delivery, then the weekly numbers, then each role, and last, your week.

line: freedom was never the reward for working harder.
caption:
I grew up as an athlete. Work harder, train longer, push through. It works in sport for a while, and in business for a while too.

Then it stops working, and most founders respond by working harder still.

My own agency and years of work on other people's brands taught me that freedom is the result of building differently. A business that grows without depending on you has to be designed that way.

One place to start: find the single thing that pulled you back in most often last month. A decision, a client, a task, a login. Design that one thing out.
